content: The recommendations have been incorporated from the 2019 WHO guideline titled Recommendations on Digital Interventions for Health System Strengthening, where they were considered context-specific. The health system must have the capacity to accept notifications and initiate appropriate health and social services, such as postnatal care services. The civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) system must be able to accept notifications, validate the information, and trigger the subsequent processes of birth registration and certification. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) made the following observations: Although evidence is limited, the GDG emphasized that birth notification is a critical first step in a cascade of care that can lead to improved and timely access to health and social services. The use of mobile devices for this purpose is likely to expedite notifications and subsequent health services. Birth notification should not replace legal birth registration but can accelerate the process by linking notifications to national civil registration systems. Digital birth notifications can help provide newborns with a legal identity and future access to health and social services. Increased notifications of births and deaths will require civil registration services to handle higher demands for registration and certification. The ability of the health system and/or CRVS system to respond to and act on birth and death notifications is essential for successful implementation. Without proper linkages, notifications would add no value and incur additional costs. The WHO postnatal care guideline aims to improve the quality of essential, routine postnatal care for women and newborns, ultimately enhancing maternal and newborn health and well-being. These recommendations must be delivered within a postnatal care model tailored to the needs of different countries, local contexts, and individual women, newborns, parents, caregivers, and families. The GDG proposed implementation considerations for each recommendation and reflected on the adoption, adaptation, and implementation of the guideline to ensure availability, accessibility, acceptability, and quality of postnatal care services for all women and newborns, in line with a human rights-based approach. Postnatal health service providers must address the needs of all individuals and their newborns equally. The WHO postnatal care model places the woman-newborn dyad at the center of care. The foundation of this model is Recommendation 44, which supports a minimum of four postnatal care contacts. The first contact involves continued care in the health facility for at least the first 24 hours after birth or a first postnatal contact within 24 hours for home births. At least three additional postnatal care contacts should occur between 48 and 72 hours, between 7 and 14 days, and during week six after birth. The overarching goal is to provide respectful, individualized, person-centered care at every contact. This includes effective clinical practices (assessments, referrals, and management), timely and relevant information, and psychosocial and emotional support by competent and motivated health workers within a well-functioning health system. An effective referral system, including communication between facilityand community-based care and between health and transport systems in case of complications, is also essential. Within this model, the term contact implies active interaction between women, newborns, parents, caregivers, and care providers. All recommendations in this document require review by national, regional, and local health system planners to ensure they are adapted, resourced, and integrated into maternal, newborn, and child health programs. The GDG highlighted the importance of the first two weeks after birth as a critical period to identify health problems and support the transition to well-woman and well-infant care. The guideline confirms the importance of postnatal care during the first 24 hours after birth, regardless of the place of birth, and recommends a minimum 24-hour stay in the health facility with continuous care and monitoring during that time (Recommendation 45). Expanded criteria before discharge have been identified to assess and manage potential problems and prepare for the transition to home (Recommendations 46 and 47). Whether the health system is set up for a home visit in the first week or the woman and newborn need to seek routine outpatient postnatal care at a health facility or in the community, national discussions are encouraged to address barriers and facilitators to ensure these critical contacts occur. A home visit for postnatal care within the first two days after birth, where feasible, is critical to reducing mortality and morbidity and supporting the transition to home. Some women and newborns will require additional contacts or referral to specialized care based on their health and needs. Health workers must collaborate as a team to address the needs of the woman and newborn during their stay in the health facility and after they return home. This requires functional relationships and communication between health workers and across different levels of the system. The GDG emphasized the importance of establishing links with health workers who will provide care and support after discharge to ensure seamless handover and transitions. One recommendation on midwifery continuity-of-care (Recommendation 49) for contexts with strong midwifery programs adds an additional level of relationship and trust-building between the team of midwives and the woman and family. Trained community health workers will also play a vital role in providing care and support in the home and linking communities and health facilities. The guideline includes new recommendations on maternal and newborn assessments, including for common maternal mental health conditions (Recommendation 18) and newborn screening for hyperbilirubinemia and eye and hearing conditions (Recommendations 26–29). Discussions are required on how to organize screening services depending on the condition and ensure that confirmatory diagnosis, subsequent treatment, rehabilitation, and follow-up are available. In humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of recommendations should consider their integration and alignment with other response strategies. Additional considerations should be made for the unique needs of women, newborns, parents, caregivers, and families in emergency settings, including their values and preferences. Context-specific tools may be required in addition to standard tools to support the implementation of recommendations in humanitarian emergencies. The guideline will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, WHO collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. It will be available on the WHO website and as a printed publication. Technical meetings will be held between WHO and stakeholders to share the recommendations and derivative products. Evidence briefs on selected recommendations will be developed for policymakers, program managers, and health workers. The executive summary and recommendations will be translated into the six United Nations languages for dissemination through WHO regional and country offices. WHO, in collaboration with other partners, will support national and subnational working groups to adopt, adapt, and implement the recommendations.
